title: Richard III
author: William Shakespeare
about:
Richard, Duke of Gloucester, opens the play alone on stage and tells the audience he is going to make himself king of England by killing every person between himself and the throne. He starts at the top of his own family. He has his brother Clarence drowned in a barrel of wine. He waits for his eldest brother, King Edward IV, to die, then has his nephews — the boy king Edward V and his younger brother — smothered in the Tower. He marries Lady Anne, whose husband and father-in-law he has just killed, by proposing to her over the corpse. He becomes Richard III, executes his own allies as they grow suspicious, and reigns for two acts of accelerating paranoia.

The play closes at Bosworth Field, where Henry Tudor — soon to be Henry VII — defeats and kills Richard, ending the Wars of the Roses and beginning the Tudor dynasty that ruled England when Shakespeare was writing. The dawn of Bosworth includes one of Shakespeare's earliest great set pieces: a procession of ghosts of everyone Richard has murdered, each visiting his tent in turn to curse him and bless Henry.

Shakespeare wrote Richard III early, probably 1592–93, as the climax of his first history-play tetralogy (the Henry VI plays and Richard III). It contains his first great solo-villain role, the part later actors from David Garrick to Laurence Olivier to Ian McKellen have built productions around. The history is Tudor propaganda — Richard was not the monster the play makes him — but the part itself is one of the most powerful Shakespeare ever wrote.

angleCards.title: Richard the actor.
angleCards.text: Richard addresses the audience from the first lines, lets us in on every plan, and performs his way through every scene. He is Shakespeare's first great metatheatrical villain — a man who knows he is in a play and uses it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Richard as Shakespeare's first great performing villain — the way he uses the audience, the asides, and the scenes as theatre to get what he wants.

angleCards.title: The wooing of Anne.
angleCards.text: Act 1, Scene 2: Richard meets the widow of the man he murdered, proposes to her over her father-in-law's corpse, and gets her to agree. It is the most audacious scene in the play and one of the most argued-about in Shakespeare.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the wooing of Anne — the scene where Richard proposes to the widow of his victim over his corpse — and decide whether Shakespeare makes it credible, and what he wants us to feel.

angleCards.title: The women.
angleCards.text: Three queens — Margaret, Elizabeth, the Duchess of York — and one widow circle the play, mourning, cursing, and finally outlasting Richard. The play gives them more space than most of Shakespeare's histories give women, and lets them deliver some of its best lines.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the women of Richard III — Queen Margaret, Queen Elizabeth, the Duchess of York, Lady Anne — and read their grief and cursing as the play's moral counterweight to Richard.

angleCards.title: Tudor propaganda and what survives it.
angleCards.text: The historical Richard was almost certainly not the hunchbacked monster Shakespeare made him. The play is the founding document of Tudor propaganda. The part is still a great part. Watch both at once.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Richard III aware of its Tudor politics — the play is propaganda — and see what survives the propaganda as drama.

cast.name: Richard, Duke of Gloucester
cast.description: Brother of King Edward IV, deformed in the play's telling — hunched, with a withered arm — and brilliant in mind and tongue. He opens the play with one of Shakespeare's most quoted soliloquies and runs five acts of murders and asides until he is killed at Bosworth. The part has been the test piece for great actors for four centuries.

cast.name: Lady Anne
cast.description: Widow of Edward, Prince of Wales, and daughter-in-law of King Henry VI — both murdered by Richard. Richard meets her at Henry VI's funeral procession in Act 1 and persuades her to marry him before the scene is over. She lives only as long as he wants her to.

cast.name: Queen Margaret
cast.description: Widow of Henry VI, the queen of the previous war, kept around by Shakespeare for one purpose: to walk into the court and curse everyone in it. She has nothing left and tells everyone exactly what is coming for them. She is right about all of it.

cast.name: Queen Elizabeth
cast.description: Wife of Edward IV, mother of the two young princes Richard has killed in the Tower. She survives Richard, mourns her sons, and is the woman Richard returns to in Act 4 to ask for her daughter's hand. The second great wooing scene of the play.

cast.name: Buckingham
cast.description: The Duke of Buckingham, Richard's right hand for the first three acts, the man who delivers London to him and orchestrates the public acclamation. He breaks with Richard when he is asked to kill the young princes, joins the rebellion, and is executed.

cast.name: Henry, Earl of Richmond
cast.description: The Tudor claimant who lands in Wales with a small force, marches across England gathering support, and defeats Richard at Bosworth Field. He has fewer than two hundred lines in the play. He is what comes next — the play's quietly endorsed alternative.

acclaim.quote: Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York.
Richard, of the great trinity of conscious villains in Shakespeare — Iago, Edmund, and himself — is the most thoroughly enjoying his villainy.

whyItMatters.title: The First Great Soliloquy
whyItMatters.body: Richard III opens with the most famous opening monologue in English drama: Richard alone on stage, telling the audience that the wars are over, his side has won, and he intends to ruin the peace because he is bored. 'Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this son of York.' Within sixty lines he has explained his deformity, his hatred of pleasure, and his plan to set his brothers against each other. The convention Shakespeare establishes here — a villain who confides in the audience, lets us know more than the other characters, and makes us complicit in his schemes by sheer charm — runs straight to Iago, to Edmund in Lear, to Falstaff in his lower mode, and out into four centuries of later drama and film. The Underwoods of House of Cards, the Tony Sopranos, the Walter Whites: they are all working in territory Richard opened up. He is the first character in English theatre who treats the audience as his closest collaborator and makes them root for him to do terrible things.

whyItMatters.title: The Wooing of Anne
whyItMatters.body: Shakespeare gives himself one of the most impossible writing problems in the canon and solves it in a single scene. Lady Anne walks across the London streets in the funeral procession of her father-in-law Henry VI, who has been murdered. Her husband, the prince, has also been murdered. Both were killed by Richard. Richard stops the procession, addresses her over the corpse, and within two hundred lines of stichomythia — line-by-line exchange — has persuaded her to accept his ring. The scene works because Shakespeare lets Anne curse Richard with every line and lets Richard answer every curse with an audacious counter; she runs out of weapons and he doesn't. At the end he turns to the audience and asks, gleefully, 'Was ever woman in this humour wooed? / Was ever woman in this humour won?' The scene is the model for every later seduction in literature that depends on the woman's own intelligence being beaten with her own logic. It is also where the play earns the right to take Richard seriously: any man who can do this on stage in five minutes is a man who could, in fact, take the English throne.

whyItMatters.title: The Ghosts at Bosworth
whyItMatters.body: The night before the final battle at Bosworth Field, Shakespeare brings the ghosts of every person Richard has murdered on stage one by one. Each ghost crosses to Richard's tent and curses him — 'Despair and die' — then crosses to Henry's tent and blesses him — 'Live and flourish' — and disappears. There are eleven of them. The scene is half ritual, half hallucination, and it is the moment the play stops being about Richard's cleverness and starts being about what catches up with him. Shakespeare uses it to do something subtle: he stages the moral judgment as theatre rather than narration. We do not hear about Richard's crimes from a chorus; we watch the victims appear and accuse. By the time the battle starts the next morning, the audience has already been told who is going to win and why, and Shakespeare can play the battle as the working-out of a verdict already delivered. The scene is one of the earliest examples of his ability to make stagecraft do the work of philosophy, and it is the moment the play turns from chronicle to tragedy.
